issues.legal_issue: A party that obtains procedural benefits by representing that connected appeals raise common issues cannot later argue, after an adverse decision in one appeal, that the decision does not govern the others.
material_facts: The parties' connected appeals arose from a common High Court judgment and presented points the appellants represented as common to all appeals.
The appellants asked the Court to consolidate the appeals and have one appeal heard and decided on the understanding that its disposition would govern the others.
The Court granted the request, and the appellants obtained procedural benefits from consolidation.
After the decision in the selected appeal went against them, the appellants argued in the remaining appeals that the decision was per incuriam and did not bind them.
issues.conclusion: The appellants could not take that inconsistent position after obtaining the benefits of the procedure they had requested.
issues.legal_principle: A litigant may not approbate and reprobate by inviting a court to proceed on a representation and, after an adverse result, disavowing that representation. The Court relied on the principle stated in Ex Parte Pratt (52 Q.B. 334), that a party cannot accept a tribunal's jurisdiction and then challenge it after losing; it applied that principle to the appellants' change of position.

predicates.connected_appeals: The proceeding involved appeals connected by a common judgment or common issues.
predicates.party_requested_consolidation_on_common_: A party asked the court to consolidate connected appeals on the representation that their issues were common and one disposition would govern them.
predicates.party_received_procedural_benefit: The party obtained a procedural advantage from the court's acceptance of that request.
predicates.party_changed_position_after_adverse_dec: After an adverse decision, the party took a position inconsistent with the representation on which the court had acted.

issues.definition: When a party in connected appeals obtains a procedural benefit by asking the court to proceed on the basis that one decision will govern them, the party cannot take an inconsistent position after that decision is adverse.

issues.legal_issue: A prior decision of the same court on indistinguishable facts and law binds the court in a later case presenting the same points.
material_facts: The earlier appeal and the remaining appeals arose from the same High Court judgment.
The appellants represented that the points in the appeals were common and that nothing required decision in one appeal that was not common to the others.
The Court found that the earlier decision had been rendered on facts and law indistinguishable from those in the remaining appeals.
issues.conclusion: The earlier decision bound the Court in the remaining appeals.
issues.legal_principle: A decision once rendered ordinarily binds the court in like cases, and a prior decision of the Court on identical facts and law binds it on the same points in a later case. The Court referred to Cassel & Co. Ltd. v. Broome, Young v. Bristol Aeroplane Co. Ltd., Nicholas v. Penny, and The Bengal Immunity Company Ltd. Case in discussing the limits of departing from precedent and the per incuriam doctrine.

predicates.later_case_before_same_court: A later case or proceeding is before the same court that decided an earlier case.
predicates.prior_decision_on_identical_facts_and_la: The earlier decision was made on facts and law indistinguishable from those in the later case.
predicates.same_points_in_issue: The later case presents the same points that the earlier decision resolved.

issues.definition: If the same court later encounters the same points on indistinguishable facts and law, its earlier decision binds it in the later case.

issues.legal_issue: A decision is not deprived of binding force as per incuriam merely because a party challenges its reasoning; the exception is confined to an obvious oversight of a plain statutory provision or binding authority that conflicts with the decision.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the decision in the earlier appeal was per incuriam and therefore did not bind the Court in the remaining appeals.
The earlier decision had considered and decided the question of civil court jurisdiction in the land-reform litigation.
The Court found no obvious inadvertence or oversight of a plain statutory provision or binding authority running counter to the earlier decision.
issues.conclusion: The earlier decision was not per incuriam and remained binding in the connected appeals.
issues.legal_principle: The per incuriam exception is narrow and applies only in an obvious, glaring case in which a decision overlooks a plain statutory provision or obligatory authority contrary to its reasoning and result. A decision is not per incuriam merely because it was not fully argued, appears to be wrong, or misinterprets a statute. The Court relied on Morelle v. Wakeling, Cassel & Co. Ltd. v. Broome, and the authorities discussed there, including Young v. Bristol Aeroplane Co. Ltd.; it also noted The Bengal Immunity Company Ltd. Case and Nicholas v. Penny in addressing the appellants' argument.

rule.if: later_connected_appeal and party_invoked_per_incuriam and prior_decision_considered_the_point and no_obvious_oversight_of_conflicting_law

predicates.later_connected_appeal: The proceeding is a later appeal connected to an appeal already decided by the same court.
predicates.party_invoked_per_incuriam: A party argued that the earlier decision should not bind because it was reached per incuriam.
predicates.prior_decision_considered_the_point: The earlier decision addressed the point that the party says was overlooked.
predicates.no_obvious_oversight_of_conflicting_law: The earlier decision did not obviously overlook a plain legal requirement or binding authority contrary to its reasoning and result.

issues.definition: In a later connected appeal, an earlier decision remains binding where the per incuriam argument is raised, the earlier decision considered the disputed point, and no obvious conflicting legal requirement or authority was overlooked.
